ABSTRACT

SPATIAL COLOCATION ANALYSIS OF MOSQUITO SPECIES ACROSS ISOKO COMMUNITIES, DELTA STATE, NIGERIA

Journal: Environment & Ecosystem Science (EES)

Author: Opoggen L, Lawal O, Noutcha MAE

This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License CC BY 4.0, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited

DOI: 10.26480/ees.02.2026.125.130

Mosquitoes are found in environments which support their survival. Spatial analysis can reveal the association between environmental attributes and mosquitoes. However, spatial association which can reveal local association between species has been rarely explored in understanding the associations between mosquitoes’ species presence across places. Spatial colocation analysis is very effectively shows significant reasons for clustering and various patterns of interaction using different models. This study measured the local pattern of spatial association among Malaria, Filariasis and Yellow Fever vectors in Delta State, Nigeria. Field surveys were conducted across the settlements in the study area. Locations were recorded, samples collected and identified. Local colocation quotients (LCQL) were computed to determine the spatial heterogeneity and association pattern of four mosquito species (Anopheles, Aedes, Culex and Mansonia) collected from some settlements surveyed in Isoko, Delta State, Nigeria. The result showed four patterns of paired association among the mosquito species across the communities sampled which are Culex- Anopheles, Culex- Aedes, Culex- Mansonia and Anopheles-Aedes. Significant colocation pattern was found between Culex – Anopheles in one location, Culex – Aedes was found in three locations, Culex – Mansonia in one location, Anopheles – Aedes was found in two locations while a significant isolated pattern was found in one location. The vectors showed appreciable patterns of association denoting common environmental characteristics responsible for survival and disease transmission. A wide-scale analysis of different regions is required to establish this finding and incorporate it into vector surveillance and control services
